clinicalPearls: Chronic cholestatic disease marked by progressive fibrosing inflammation and stricturing of intra- and/or extrahepatic bile ducts
Strongly linked to inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis; colitis may be quiescent or diagnosed after PSC
Predominantly affects young to middle-aged men; often discovered incidentally via persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase
Fluctuating cholestatic pattern (elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT) is typical, with variable bilirubin depending on stricture burden
Cholangiography (MRCP preferred over ERCP for initial diagnosis) shows characteristic multifocal strictures alternating with normal or dilated segments (beaded appearance)
Any patient with IBD and unexplained cholestatic liver tests should be evaluated for PSC
Carries increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, and colorectal cancer (in those with concurrent colitis)
No medical therapy has been proven to alter the natural history; liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment for advanced disease
harrison.pathophysiology: PSC is thought to result from an immune-mediated process in genetically susceptible individuals, possibly triggered by altered gut permeability and microbial translocation related to colonic inflammation, leading to periductal inflammation and concentric fibrosis of bile ducts. Progressive fibro-obliteration produces multifocal strictures with intervening dilations, eventually causing biliary obstruction, secondary bacterial cholangitis, and biliary cirrhosis. The disease can involve both intra- and extrahepatic ducts, and a small-duct variant exists without visible cholangiographic changes.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis (from prior surgery, ischemia, or stones)
Autoimmune hepatitis (including overlap syndrome with PSC)
additionalInvestigations: Alkaline phosphatase and GGT - screen for and monitor cholestasis
MRCP - noninvasive imaging of choice to visualize characteristic ductal beading and strictures
ERCP - reserved for cases needing therapeutic intervention or when MRCP is nondiagnostic
Liver biopsy - helpful mainly for suspected small-duct PSC or overlap with autoimmune hepatitis; may show onion-skin periductal fibrosis
Serum IgG4 - to exclude IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
Colonoscopy with biopsies - to evaluate for concurrent inflammatory bowel disease
CA 19-9 and repeat cross-sectional imaging - surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma in patients with dominant strictures or clinical deterioration
Autoantibody panel (ANA, ASMA, p-ANCA) - supportive workup, though p-ANCA lacks specificity
redFlags: Rapid clinical deterioration, weight loss, or new dominant stricture - raise concern for cholangiocarcinoma
Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain suggesting superimposed acute bacterial cholangitis
Marked rise in CA 19-9 or new mass on imaging
New-onset or worsening ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy indicating progression to cirrhosis and decompensation
Colonic dysplasia or malignancy found on surveillance colonoscopy in patients with concurrent IBD
pitfalls: Attributing isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation in an IBD patient to the bowel disease alone without pursuing cholangiographic evaluation
Missing small-duct PSC, which has a normal cholangiogram and requires biopsy for diagnosis
Failing to distinguish IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, which is often steroid-responsive, from classic PSC
Underestimating cholangiocarcinoma risk and not maintaining surveillance in long-standing disease
harrison.prognosis: PSC follows a variable but generally progressive course over years to decades, often culminating in biliary cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease; median transplant-free survival historically has been reported around a decade or more from diagnosis, though course varies widely between patients. Cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer (in those with IBD) are major contributors to morbidity and mortality.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Chapter on Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts / Sclerosing Cholangitis
